title: What To Do When You Realize You've Lost Control Of Your Class ntrol-of-your-class/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the difficult moment when a teacher must admit they have lost control of their class, and offers a two-step process to regain it within about 30 minutes. Step one is to firmly take a stand: get students seated and quiet through patient, repeated insistence, then wait in silence — without visible frustration — until true quiet is achieved, followed by an additional five minutes of silence to make the shift felt. Step two is to teach one common routine, like lining up, with exacting standards and no explanation, sending students back to redo it if it isn't done well. He frames this as a reset moment, an intervention that reestablishes the teacher's standards from a single successful routine. The piece closes with the reminder to return to this reset any time control starts slipping again.
points: Recognizing you've genuinely lost control of your class, rather than blaming external factors, is the necessary first step to fixing it.
Step one is patiently getting students seated and silent, then waiting in silence — without visible frustration — an extra five minutes after quiet is achieved.
Step two is teaching one common routine, like lining up, to an exacting standard without explanation, sending students back to redo it if imperfect.
This reset can be applied any time a class starts running loose, not just once at the start of the year.
Building one successful routine creates a foundation to build additional structure and respect from.
quotes: No, the problem is that you’ve lost control of your class. But once you come to grips with this realization, once you decide you no longer want to teach in a stressful, chaotic environment, you can start doing something about it.
In fact, with the following strategy you can walk into any classroom and have the students calm and following your directions within 30 minutes.
Once you have your students seated, have them clear their desks so there are no distractions, and then simply ask them to be quiet.
Once your students are quiet, I recommend waiting in silence another five minutes after the last voice is heard.
For most classrooms, lining up to leave the room is the perfect routine because it happens every day and there are multiple opportunities for misbehavior.
Send your students back to their desks. Wait until you have their attention and respect. And then make them prove themselves once again.
